findings.stat_label: your NSF fee vs peer median
findings.headline: Your NSF fee is double the peer median.
findings.body: At $30.00, your returned-item fee is 2x the median of 34 peer banks — the 82nd percentile. A quarter of your cohort now charges $6.25 or less as the industry retreats from NSF fees under regulatory scrutiny. It is the one conspicuous line on an otherwise customer-friendly schedule.

findings.headline: You are the cheapest bank in the room — quietly.
findings.body: Paper statements ($0.25 vs a $3.58 median, 7th percentile), cashier's checks ($3 vs $5.50, 8th percentile — the cohort minimum), incoming domestic wires ($5 vs $12.50, 17th percentile), and card replacement ($5 vs $10) all sit at or near the bottom of your cohort. That is a genuine low-fee story no one is telling.

findings.headline: Three benchmark categories are invisible to comparison.
findings.body: Overdraft, monthly maintenance, and deposited-item-return fees did not appear in your published schedule data. In an era when fee schedules are scraped and compared, an unpublished fee reads as either a hidden fee or a missed chance to show pricing that — given the rest of your schedule — is probably competitive.

exec_narrative: Net position: First Bank runs a barbell. One side is a $30 NSF fee at double the median of 34 comparable banks — the 82nd percentile and the single line most likely to draw attention. The other side is a service-fee stack priced at or near the cohort floor: paper statements, cashier's checks, incoming wires, and card replacement all sit in the bottom third of peers, several at the literal minimum. Three core categories are missing from the published data entirely. The pricing conversation writes itself: decide the NSF fee deliberately, publish the missing lines, and start taking credit for the low-fee posture you already have.

callouts.title: NSF / returned item — $30.00
callouts.body: Your NSF fee is exactly double the peer median, and the distribution is moving away from you — a quarter of comparable banks now charge $6.25 or less as institutions retire returned-item fees ahead of regulatory and reputational pressure. Whether the answer is a cut, a cap, or a documented rationale, this line deserves a decision rather than a default, because it is the fee most likely to appear in a local fee survey next to your name.

callouts.title: Service fees — a bottom-decile stack, marketed nowhere
callouts.stat: Paper statement $0.25 vs $3.58 (P7) · Cashier's check $3 vs $5.50 (P8) · Incoming wire $5 vs $12.50 (P17) · Card replacement $5 vs $10 (P31)
callouts.body: Four consumer-facing service fees sit at or near the bottom of your cohort — two at the cohort minimum. Competitors' own published schedules substantiate a 'lower everyday fees than most banks' claim. If deliberate, this belongs in your marketing; if not deliberate, it is margin available without touching the NSF headline.

callouts.title: Unpublished fees — overdraft, maintenance, deposited item return
callouts.stat: 3 of 15 benchmark categories flagged as data gaps · peer medians $30.00 / $12.00 / $12.00
callouts.body: The categories missing from your published data include overdraft — the most scrutinized consumer fee in banking. Peers publish these lines and get compared on them; you don't and can't. Publishing converts an information gap into a transparency point, and given how the rest of your schedule prices, the comparison would likely flatter you.

context_narrative:
Two currents define the fee landscape your schedule competes in. First, the retreat from NSF: large banks have largely eliminated returned-item fees, and the pressure has migrated down-market — visible in your own cohort, where the NSF median ($15) sits at half your posted fee and a quarter of peers charge $6.25 or less. Second, published fee schedules have become marketing documents: they are public, scraped, and compared, which turns every outlier line into a small reputational bet and every unpublished line into an open question.

Mid-sized community banks sit in an exposed middle: large enough to show up in comparisons and examiner conversations, without the brand gravity that lets the largest institutions price premiums quietly. In that position, the highest-leverage moves are surgical — resolve the one conspicuous outlier, close the publication gaps, and actively advertise a service-fee stack that already prices at the bottom of the cohort.
